source.title: Evidence of Learned Look-Ahead in a Chess-Playing Neural Network
source.authors: Erik Jenner; Shreyas Kapur; V. Georgiev; Cameron S. Allen; Scott Emmons; Stuart Russell

record.tranche_reason: Tests learned look-ahead in chess, a new task and architecture relative to language-model look-ahead work, using causal interventions and probing.
record.gate_note: Reports causal effects from patching future-move squares and ablating attention pathways, plus future-move probe accuracy. These are results bearing on chess look-ahead. Other cited work is not counted as this study's results.
record.test_reason: Tests internal look-ahead in a non-language setting: the Leela chess policy transformer, a bidirectional model with no autoregression. It uses its own activation patching, attention ablations and a bilinear probe on future-move squares, reporting causal effects on the model's move choice. This bears directly on V5 (chess named). No language-model, rhyme, single-hidden-state token-decoding or pre-caching results, so V1–V4 are untested. V6 is not directly tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors claim correlational and causal evidence that some form of look-ahead plays an important role in Leela's policy in many tactically complex states. They call this an existence proof. They lack a precise account of the algorithm, do not test comparison of multiple lines, and draw no direct conclusion about LLMs.
record.recipe_differences: Chess-policy-network analysis rather than next-token language modeling; uses square-level activation patching, attention ablation, and a bilinear probe to study future moves.
record.method_sensitivity: Effects vary by layer: the 3rd-move target is important around layers 10–11, while the 1st-move target dominates later. Results are generally stronger when the 1st- and 2nd-move target squares coincide than when they differ.
record.problems: The dataset is filtered to 22.5k puzzles chosen to be difficult for a weaker model and correctly solved by Leela, so results do not establish how often look-ahead occurs across the general input distribution. The study follows a single principal variation and does not test comparison of multiple lines. The exact implementation is not identified; the authors note possible unknown systematic errors beyond the reported statistical uncertainty.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant reported outcomes left out.

untested.parts: Multi-step reasoning in language models, Sokoban, and other architectures. Look-ahead outside the filtered hard-puzzle set (the authors do not claim it occurs in every state). Search over multiple lines of play. Other Leela versions or chess networks.

Not directly tested. The study's corruptions are chosen to target non-heuristic mechanisms, and look-ahead reaches only the 3rd ply. It does not compare plan depth or heuristic explanations in the way V6 frames them.
All: no language model or verse.
All: the probe is a bilinear form over two squares' activations predicting a future move, not future tokens from a single hidden state in an autoregressive LM.
All: no open-weight language models or rhyme.

missing.what: Subsplit results: all effects much stronger when the 1st and 2nd move targets coincide. On the different-targets split, the L12H12 baseline ablation exceeds the main 3rd→1st ablation. Ablating 3rd→2nd target flow has an even smaller effect.
2nd-move (opponent reply) squares are not unusually important in patching; the authors are unsure why.
Layer dependence: the 3rd-move target matters around L10–11, the 1st-move target dominates after L12. Probe accuracy rises through the layers.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The record's second limits_scope label (single-line, filtered puzzles, no search) describes untested parts rather than qualifying results, so it was moved to untested. A results-based limits_scope was added for the different-targets split from Appendix G. Control rows were re-marked cannot_determine because they are baselines, not tests. Dataset and corruption selection are both filtered by a weaker model to favour look-ahead, which biases toward finding it.

versions.untested_parts: Rhyme planning and interventions on rhyme words in a language model.
The probe predicts a chess move using a bilinear form over activations at multiple squares, not tokens several positions ahead from a single hidden state.
Autoregressive language-model pre-caching or breadcrumbs. Leela uses bidirectional attention over board squares and has no autoregressive prediction.
Rhyme planning in open-weight language models using open attribution-graph or probing tools.
The study tests chess only, on one Leela network and a filtered set of difficult puzzles. It does not test multi-step reasoning or Sokoban, or other tasks and architectures.

Whether planning is merely a shallow/local heuristic or an incidental feature that does not steer generation. The study reports causal effects in chess, but does not directly compare planning against those alternatives.

rows.subject: T82-768x15x24h
rows.stage_stated: finetuned to behave the same whether or not history was passed in; originally supervised on MCTS roll-outs produced by an earlier model
rows.operation_detail: Patched activations from a corrupted puzzle into the clean forward pass on the 3rd-move target square.
rows.measure: Reduction in log odds of the ground-truth best move
rows.note: The paper says this corresponds to a probability reduction such as 50% to 13%; the reported effect is an average over the puzzle dataset.

rows.subject: T82-768x15x24h
rows.stage_stated: finetuned to behave the same whether or not history was passed in; originally supervised on MCTS roll-outs produced by an earlier model
rows.operation_detail: For each puzzle, patched the square with the largest effect among the 61 squares other than the 1st-move target, 3rd-move target, or corrupted square; averaged the per-puzzle maxima.
rows.measure: Reduction in log odds of the ground-truth best move
rows.note: The paper contrasts this maximum over 61 other squares with the 1.88 reduction for the 3rd-move target.
rows.check: Control/baseline for r1, not a test of look-ahead. The value 0.55 is a nonzero per-puzzle maximum over 61 squares, so 'absent' misdescribes it. Its role is the comparison showing r1's 1.88 is outsized.

rows.subject: T82-768x15x24h
rows.stage_stated: finetuned to behave the same whether or not history was passed in; originally supervised on MCTS roll-outs produced by an earlier model
rows.operation_detail: Patched the output of one attention head at a time from the corrupted to the clean forward pass.
rows.measure: Mean reduction in log odds of the ground-truth best move
rows.value: figure only; text says this head has a much larger average effect than any other attention head
rows.note: The text identifies L12H12 as the head that stands out; numerical values are only plotted.

rows.subject: T82-768x15x24h
rows.stage_stated: finetuned to behave the same whether or not history was passed in; originally supervised on MCTS roll-outs produced by an earlier model
rows.operation_detail: Measured the attention-pattern entry whose query is the 1st-move target and key is the 3rd-move target in L12H12.
rows.measure: Fraction of puzzles where this entry was larger than all 4095 other attention entries in the head
rows.note: The authors interpret this as the head often moving information from the 3rd-move target toward the 1st-move target.
rows.check: No baseline stated. Chance that one entry is the maximum of 4096 is ~0.02%, so 29.8% is far above chance. The authors call it anecdotal.

rows.subject: T82-768x15x24h
rows.stage_stated: finetuned to behave the same whether or not history was passed in; originally supervised on MCTS roll-outs produced by an earlier model
rows.operation_detail: Zeroed the single L12H12 attention entry from the 3rd-move target key to the 1st-move target query.
rows.measure: Reduction in log odds of the correct move; fraction of puzzles exceeding a reduction threshold
rows.value: Reduction greater than 1.5 in more than 10% of puzzles
rows.uncertainty: 95% CIs shown in Figure 5; numerical interval not stated in text
rows.note: The paper says this is much larger than ablating all 4095 other attention weights together.

rows.subject: T82-768x15x24h
rows.stage_stated: finetuned to behave the same whether or not history was passed in; originally supervised on MCTS roll-outs produced by an earlier model
rows.operation_detail: Zeroed all 4095 L12H12 attention entries other than the 3rd-to-1st target entry.
rows.measure: Reduction in log odds of the correct move
rows.value: figure only; text says the effect is much smaller than ablating the single 3rd-to-1st target entry
rows.uncertainty: 95% CIs shown in Figure 5; numerical interval not stated in text
rows.note: The plotted distribution is the comparison baseline for the targeted single-entry ablation.
rows.check: Control ablation (all 4095 other L12H12 entries), used as the comparison for r5. Marking it 'absent' risks reading it as evidence against V5. Also, on the different-targets split this baseline exceeds the main ablation (Appendix G).

rows.subject: T82-768x15x24h
rows.stage_stated: finetuned to behave the same whether or not history was passed in; originally supervised on MCTS roll-outs produced by an earlier model
rows.operation_detail: Trained a bilinear probe on residual-stream activations to predict the 3rd-move target square, using the 1st-move target square as input.

relationships.condition: Leela T82-768x15x24h policy net on 22.5k filtered hard Lichess puzzles (all puzzles pooled)
relationships.reason: 3rd-move target patching cuts log odds by 1.88 vs 0.55 for other squares. A single L12H12 3rd→1st entry ablation has large effects. Piece-head ablation reduces log odds ≥1.5 in 60% of puzzles. Probe accuracy is 92% vs 15% random (r1, r3, r4, r5, r7, r10).
relationships.display_finding: Patching third-move targets reduced log odds by 1.88 versus 0.55 for other squares, ablating one L12H12 attention entry substantially changed choices, piece-head ablation reduced log odds by at least 1.5 in 60% of puzzles, and probes achieved 92% accuracy versus 15% random.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Leela T82-768x15x24h policy net on 22.5k filtered hard Lichess puzzles (all puzzles pooled)
source_check.reason: Pooled patching, L12H12 interventions, and probing support internal look-ahead. The r7 result is additional evidence restricted to puzzles with principal variations longer than three moves; its 60% rate is not a pooled-dataset rate.

relationships.condition: Puzzles where 1st and 2nd move target squares differ (17% of the dataset)
relationships.reason: Per Appendix G text (no row), effects are much weaker on this split. There the L12H12 baseline ablation beats the 3rd→1st entry ablation, so the L12H12 pathway (r5) is specific to the sacrifice-type puzzles.
relationships.display_finding: Effects were much weaker in the 17% of puzzles with different first- and second-move targets, where baseline L12H12 ablation exceeded third-to-first-entry ablation, indicating a pathway specific to sacrifice-type puzzles.

tranche.reason: Tests internal look-ahead in a new setting: a bidirectional chess policy transformer, using activation patching, attention ablation, and probing.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased: evidence for some look-ahead, without a precise algorithm, multiple-line search test, or direct LLM conclusion. The supplied text is arXiv v1 and does not verify later review status.

statements.correction: Piece-head ablation: log-odds reduction ≥1.5 in 60% of puzzles whose principal variation is longer than three moves (Section 3.2; Figure 7). Other reported numerical results match. Supplied text identifies itself as a preprint under review.
statements.problem: The 60% result is presented under the overall 22.5k-puzzle condition without its restricted experimental subset. NeurIPS review status cannot be established from this preprint.

statements.correction: Piece-head ablation: log-odds reduction ≥1.5 in 60% of puzzles with principal variations longer than three moves (Section 3.2; Figure 7). Other numerical results and the different-target qualification match. Supplied text identifies itself as a preprint under review.
statements.problem: The 60% piece-head result omits its principal-variation-length restriction. The supplied text cannot establish NeurIPS review status or the comparative strongest-test ranking.
